tip: For a stretch of time, Swedish uses i: duschar i tio minuter = showers for ten minutes.

english: You can swim for free here.
tip: Man is the general you or one: man får bada = you may swim. It always takes a singular verb, får.

english: A cat is sitting in the window.
tip: Swedish states the posture of things: a cat placed there sitter (sits) rather than just is. En katt sitter i fönstret.

target: Vi kommer inte att vara sena.
tip: Kommer att marks the future: kommer att vara = will be. The negation slots in between: kommer inte att vara sena.

target: Sätt dig ner på morgonen ofta!
english: Sit down in the morning often!
tip: Reflexive imperatives: sätt dig (sit down), skynda dig (hurry up). "Dig" for 'yourself.'

target: I och för sig har du rätt.
tip: "I och för sig" = in itself / admittedly – very common hedging phrase.

target: Jag visste inte att du var här.
english: I didn't know you were here.
tip: Visste is the irregular past of veta (to know): jag visste inte = I didn't know. No -de ending is added.

target: Jag vet att han inte bor här.
english: I know that he doesn't live here.
tip: Inside an att-clause, inte comes before the verb: att han inte bor här. In a main clause it would be han bor inte.

target: Vi får se vad som händer på jobbet.
english: We'll see what happens at work.
tip: When vad is the subject of the next clause, Swedish adds som: vad som händer = what happens. The som cannot be dropped.

target: Eftersom vi inte hade pengar stannade vi hemma.
english: Since we didn't have money we stayed home.
tip: Begin with a clause like eftersom ..., and the main verb still comes second, flipping ahead of the subject: stannade vi hemma.
Swedes often say "det ordnar sig" to express calm optimism about the future.
Reflexive pronoun "sig" is used for third person: "Han tvättar sig" = He washes himself.
For body parts Swedish uses the definite form, not a possessive: ansiktet (the face) means my face when the owner is obvious.
"Vakna" is not reflexive in Swedish, unlike in some other languages.
Kanske can trigger verb-second: Kanske kommer han means maybe he comes, with the verb before the subject.
Swedish says i telefon (in the phone) for on the phone, using i where English uses on.
lära sig means to learn; lära without sig means to teach. Here lärt sig marks learning, not teaching.
Use mitt (not min) before ett-words: fel is an ett-word, so it is mitt fel, my fault.
To want a thing, Swedish says vill ha (will have), not vill alone: vill ha means want to have.
sina means one's own and points back to the subject: sina ögon are his own eyes, not someone else's.
tycka om means to like, and it splits: inte lands between the two parts, tyckte inte om.
"Inte heller" = neither/nor. "Inte heller jag" = me neither.

english: She has no time at all.
tip: "Inte alls" = not at all – a common intensifier for negation.

target: De har inte bestämt sig än.
tip: "Än" (yet) goes at the end of negative sentences.

target: Om du inte vill, behöver du inte.
english: If you don't want to, you don't have to.
tip: In an om (if) clause, inte comes before the verb: om du inte vill, not om du vill inte.

target: Nästa vecka börjar den nya kursen på universitetet.
english: Next week the new course at the university begins.
tip: Start with a time phrase and the verb still comes second: Nästa vecka börjar puts börjar before the subject.

target: Vi bor på landet nära en liten by.
english: We live in the countryside near a small village.
tip: på landet means in the countryside, not on the land; landet here is rural areas, not a nation.

target: Vi har känt varandra sedan vi var små barn.
english: We have known each other since we were small children.
tip: varandra means each other, the reciprocal pronoun: känt varandra is have known each other.

target: Hon har jobbat som läkare i över femton år nu.
english: She has worked as a doctor for over fifteen years now.
tip: No article before a profession after som: jobbat som läkare, worked as a doctor, drops the a.

english: I comb my hair in front of the mirror.
tip: Daily routine verbs are often reflexive: kammar mig (comb myself), klär mig (dress myself).
